mn25:1.2: At one time the Blessed One was staying at Sāvatthi in Jeta’s Grove, Anāthapiṇḍika’s monastery.
mn25:1.3: There the Blessed One addressed the monks:
mn25:2.1: “Monks, a hunter does not lay out bait for deer with the thought:
mn25:2.2: ‘May these deer eat this bait I have laid out and live long, be beautiful, and endure for a long time.’
mn25:2.3: Instead, monks, a hunter lays out bait for deer with the thought:
mn25:2.4: ‘May these deer eat this bait I have laid out, and eating it greedily, become intoxicated. Being intoxicated, may they become negligent. Being negligent, may they do as I wish in this baited trap.’
mn25:3.1: Then, monks, the first group of deer ate the bait laid out by the hunter, eating it greedily. Eating it greedily, they became intoxicated. Being intoxicated, they became negligent. Being negligent, they did as the hunter wished in that baited trap.
mn25:3.2: Thus, monks, the first group of deer did not escape the hunter’s power.
mn25:4.1: Then, monks, the second group of deer thought:
mn25:4.2: ‘The first group of deer ate the bait laid out by the hunter, eating it greedily. Eating it greedily, they became intoxicated. Being intoxicated, they became negligent. Being negligent, they did as the hunter wished in that baited trap.
mn25:4.3: Thus, the first group of deer did not escape the hunter’s power.
mn25:4.4: What if we were to completely abstain from eating the bait and, living in fear, dwell in the forest?’
mn25:4.5: So they completely abstained from eating the bait and, living in fear, dwelled in the forest.
mn25:4.6: At the end of the hot season, when the grass and water had dried up, their bodies became very thin.
mn25:4.7: With their bodies very thin, their strength and energy diminished.
mn25:4.8: With their strength and energy diminished, they returned to that bait laid out by the hunter.
mn25:4.9: There they ate the bait greedily.
mn25:4.10: Eating it greedily, they became intoxicated. Being intoxicated, they became negligent. Being negligent, they did as the hunter wished in that baited trap.
mn25:4.11: Thus, monks, the second group of deer also did not escape the hunter’s power.

mn25:5.2: ‘The first group of deer ate the bait laid out by the hunter...
mn25:5.3: Thus, the first group of deer did not escape the hunter’s power.
mn25:5.4: The second group of deer thought:
mn25:5.5: ‘The first group of deer ate the bait laid out by the hunter...
mn25:5.6: Thus, the first group of deer did not escape the hunter’s power.
mn25:5.7: What if we were to completely abstain from eating the bait and, living in fear, dwell in the forest?’
mn25:5.8: So they completely abstained from eating the bait and, living in fear, dwelled in the forest.
mn25:5.9: At the end of the hot season, when the grass and water had dried up, their bodies became very thin.
mn25:5.10: With their bodies very thin, their strength and energy diminished.
mn25:5.11: With their strength and energy diminished, they returned to that bait laid out by the hunter.
mn25:5.12: There they ate the bait greedily.
mn25:5.13: Eating it greedily, they became intoxicated. Being intoxicated, they became negligent. Being negligent, they did as the hunter wished in that baited trap.
mn25:5.14: Thus, monks, the second group of deer also did not escape the hunter’s power.
mn25:5.15: What if we were to make a dwelling near the bait laid out by the hunter?
mn25:5.16: Having made a dwelling there, we could eat the bait laid out by the hunter without greed, without becoming intoxicated. Eating without greed, without becoming intoxicated, we would not become negligent. Not becoming negligent, we would not do as the hunter wishes in that baited trap.’
mn25:5.17: So they made a dwelling near the bait laid out by the hunter.
mn25:5.18: Having made a dwelling there, they ate the bait laid out by the hunter without greed, without becoming intoxicated. Eating without greed, without becoming intoxicated, they did not become negligent. Not becoming negligent, they did not do as the hunter wished in that baited trap.
mn25:5.19: Then, monks, it occurred to the hunter and his companions:
mn25:5.20: ‘These third group of deer are cunning and deceitful. They are powerful and have outsmarted us. They are eating the bait laid out and we do not know their coming or going.
mn25:5.21: What if we were to surround this bait laid out with large sticks and branches, perhaps we will see the dwelling of the third group of deer, where they go.’
mn25:5.22: So they surrounded the bait laid out with large sticks and branches.
mn25:5.23: The hunter and his companions saw the dwelling of the third group of deer, where they went.
mn25:5.24: Thus, monks, the third group of deer also did not escape the hunter’s power.

mn25:6.34: So they surrounded the bait laid out with large sticks and branches.
mn25:6.35: The hunter and his companions did not see the dwelling of the fourth group of deer, where they went.
mn25:6.36: Then, monks, it occurred to the hunter and his companions:
mn25:6.37: ‘If we disturb the fourth group of deer, they will disturb others, and those disturbed will disturb still others. Thus, all the deer will escape from this baited trap.
mn25:6.38: What if we were to ignore the fourth group of deer?’
mn25:6.39: So the hunter and his companions ignored the fourth group of deer.
mn25:6.40: Thus, monks, the fourth group of deer escaped the hunter’s power.
mn25:7.1: This is an analogy I have made to convey a meaning.
mn25:7.3: ‘Bait,’ monks, is a term for the five strands of sensual pleasure.
mn25:7.4: ‘Hunter,’ monks, is a term for Mara the Evil One.
mn25:7.5: ‘Hunter’s companions,’ monks, is a term for Mara’s followers.
mn25:7.6: ‘Deer,’ monks, is a term for ascetics and brahmins.
mn25:8.1: There, monks, the first group of ascetics and brahmins ate the bait laid out by Mara and these worldly pleasures, eating it greedily.
mn25:8.2: Eating it greedily, they became intoxicated. Being intoxicated, they became negligent. Being negligent, they did as Mara wished in that baited trap and these worldly pleasures.
mn25:8.3: Thus, monks, the first group of ascetics and brahmins did not escape Mara’s power.
mn25:8.4: Just as the first group of deer, monks, I say the first group of ascetics and brahmins are like that.
mn25:9.1: There, monks, the second group of ascetics and brahmins thought:
mn25:9.2: ‘The first group of ascetics and brahmins ate the bait laid out by Mara and these worldly pleasures, eating it greedily.
mn25:9.3: Eating it greedily, they became intoxicated. Being intoxicated, they became negligent. Being negligent, they did as Mara wished in that baited trap and these worldly pleasures.
mn25:9.4: Thus, the first group of ascetics and brahmins did not escape Mara’s power.
mn25:9.5: What if we were to completely abstain from eating the bait and these worldly pleasures, living in fear, dwell in the forest?’
mn25:9.6: So they completely abstained from eating the bait and these worldly pleasures, living in fear, dwelled in the forest.
mn25:9.7: They lived on vegetables, millet, wild rice, hide-parings, moss, rice bran, rice scum, sesame flour, grass, cow dung, eating forest roots and fruits, and living on fallen fruits.
mn25:9.8: At the end of the hot season, when the grass and water had dried up, their bodies became very thin.
mn25:9.9: With their bodies very thin, their strength and energy diminished.
mn25:9.10: With their strength and energy diminished, their mental liberation diminished.
mn25:9.11: With their mental liberation diminished, they returned to that bait laid out by Mara and these worldly pleasures.
mn25:9.12: There they ate the bait greedily.
mn25:9.13: Eating it greedily, they became intoxicated. Being intoxicated, they became negligent. Being negligent, they did as Mara wished in that baited trap and these worldly pleasures.
mn25:9.14: Thus, monks, the second group of ascetics and brahmins also did not escape Mara’s power.
mn25:9.15: Just as the second group of deer, monks, I say the second group of ascetics and brahmins are like that.

mn25:10.20: And they held such views as these:
mn25:10.21: ‘The world is eternal,’ or ‘The world is not eternal,’
mn25:10.22: ‘The world is finite,’ or ‘The world is infinite,’
mn25:10.23: ‘The soul and the body are the same,’ or ‘The soul is one thing and the body another,’
mn25:10.24: ‘The Tathagata exists after death,’ or ‘The Tathagata does not exist after death,’ or ‘The Tathagata both exists and does not exist after death,’ or ‘The Tathagata neither exists nor does not exist after death.’
mn25:10.25: Thus, monks, the third group of ascetics and brahmins also did not escape Mara’s power.
mn25:10.26: Just as the third group of deer, monks, I say the third group of ascetics and brahmins are like that.

mn25:12.1: And how, monks, is it a place where Mara and his followers cannot go?
mn25:12.2: Here, monks, a monk, quite secluded from sensual pleasures, secluded from unwholesome states, enters upon and abides in the first jhana, which is accompanied by applied and sustained thought, with rapture and pleasure born of seclusion.
mn25:12.3: This is called a monk who has blinded Mara, has become invisible to the Evil One by depriving Mara’s eye of its opportunity.
mn25:13.1: Again, monks, with the stilling of applied and sustained thought, a monk enters upon and abides in the second jhana, which has self-confidence and singleness of mind without applied and sustained thought, with rapture and pleasure born of concentration.
mn25:13.2: This is called a monk who has blinded Mara...
mn25:14.1: Again, monks, with the fading away of rapture, a monk abides in equanimity, and mindful and fully aware, still feeling pleasure with the body, he enters upon and abides in the third jhana, on account of which noble ones announce: ‘He has a pleasant abiding who has equanimity and is mindful.’
mn25:14.2: This is called a monk who has blinded Mara...
mn25:15.1: Again, monks, with the abandoning of pleasure and pain, and with the previous disappearance of joy and grief, a monk enters upon and abides in the fourth jhana, which has neither-pain-nor-pleasure and purity of mindfulness due to equanimity.
mn25:15.2: This is called a monk who has blinded Mara...
mn25:16.1: Again, monks, with the complete transcending of perceptions of form, with the disappearance of perceptions of sensory impact, with non-attention to perceptions of diversity, aware that ‘space is infinite,’ a monk enters upon and abides in the base of infinite space.
mn25:16.2: This is called a monk who has blinded Mara...
mn25:17.1: Again, monks, by completely transcending the base of infinite space, aware that ‘consciousness is infinite,’ a monk enters upon and abides in the base of infinite consciousness.
mn25:17.2: This is called a monk who has blinded Mara...
mn25:18.1: Again, monks, by completely transcending the base of infinite consciousness, aware that ‘there is nothing,’ a monk enters upon and abides in the base of nothingness.
mn25:18.2: This is called a monk who has blinded Mara...
mn25:19.1: Again, monks, by completely transcending the base of nothingness, a monk enters upon and abides in the base of neither perception nor non-perception.
mn25:19.2: This is called a monk who has blinded Mara...
mn25:20.1: Again, monks, by completely transcending the base of neither perception nor non-perception, a monk enters upon and abides in the cessation of perception and feeling. And his taints are destroyed by his seeing with wisdom.
mn25:20.2: This is called a monk who has blinded Mara, has become invisible to the Evil One by depriving Mara’s eye of its opportunity, and has crossed over attachment to the world.
mn25:20.3: This is what the Blessed One said.
mn25:20.4: The monks were satisfied and delighted in the Blessed One’s words.
mn25:20.5: The Discourse on the Bait is finished.
